The Thames River. England's most important river, flowing two hundred and fifteen miles through south-central England to the North Sea. It is London's lifeline. The city was founded at a Thames ford, and the river shaped England's maritime power and colonial expansion.

The Thames originates in the Cotswold Hills and flows southeast through London before widening into a tidal estuary leading to the North Sea. London's position at the Thames's first tidal crossing made it a natural trade hub. Roman Londinium was established here as a port because of this geographical advantage. The Thames provided London's water supply and powered mills throughout the medieval period. Medieval London's prosperity was inseparable from the river and the commerce it enabled.

The tidal Thames historically froze solid during severe winters, supporting Frost Fairs where ice-bound festivals and markets occurred on the frozen river surface. The last recorded Frost Fair took place in eighteen thirteen. The thirteenth-century Magna Carta was signed at Runnymede, a Thames-side meadow in the countryside west of London. The Thames valley hosted England's most important political moments. Greenwich and Hampton Court, royal residences on the Thames, showcased power and culture. The river was England's principal transport for royalty and goods moving throughout the kingdom.

The Thames is the defining river of English geography and history. The city of London was founded by the Thames and grew wealthy through river commerce. The river shaped the formation and growth of the United Kingdom, and its influence extended to Britain's naval and commercial power worldwide. The Thames's location at this crucial point shaped Britain's emergence as the capital of the world's greatest naval power.
